newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Zapatistas to mull renewing peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Zapatistas to mull renewing peace talks.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-10-14

text.p: Mexican Zapatista rebels are scheduled to meet Congressional peace mediators on Tuesday in an attempt to restart stalled peace talks in the southern state of Chiapas, legislators said on Monday.

The negotiations were to take place with an all-party Congressional mediating body known as Cocopa that is being used by the government to shepherd the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN) back into peace talks.
The EZLN, which launched a Maya Indian rebellion in January 1994, suspended 18 months of stop-and-go peace talks in September, accusing the government of negotiating in bad faith.

But it appeared to have offered to discuss ways of returning to the negotiating table as part of a bargain last week in which the rebels were given permission to send a delegate to a high-profile Indian forum in Mexico City.
"The commission will travel on Tuesday to San Cristobal de Las Casas for a reunion with the EZLN," said federal Deputy Cesar Chavez, a member of Cocopa.

He said Zapatista leader Subcommander Marcos was slated to attend the talks. Marcos led the rebels in tense negotiations with Cocopa last week that ended with permission for an ailing guerrilla leader, Commander Ramona, to head to Mexico City.
Previously, the government had threatened to arrest guerrilla leaders if they sought to attend the forum.

Ramona became the first Zapatista leader to be allowed out of Chiapas during more than 2-1/2 years of rebel tension in the state, and was given a festive reception by supporters during a rally in the main square of the capital last weekend.

A decision by the rebels to renew peace negotiations would be considered a feather in the cap of the government of President Ernesto Zedillo. It has become increasingly anxious to make peace in Chiapas since rival rebels, the Popular Revolutionary Army, took up arms in June in other southern states.
